title: The unknown god (Acts 17:22–31)
hookLine: in Athens Paul says in him we live and move and are

cards: Athens. Even in Paul's day it was a kind of university town, well-known for its past, full of temples, statues and people arguing in the marketplace.

Paul is waiting there for his friends, walking the streets, and the city's statues stir him deeply. Philosophers hear him talking about Jesus and the resurrection and say, what is this babbler trying to say?
So they bring him to the Areopagus, the hill where Athens heard new ideas, and ask him to explain. And Paul doesn't begin by attacking anyone.

teach.b: He begins with something he saw on his walk. Men of Athens, I see you are very religious. As I passed by, I found an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown God."
What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you. That's his doorway: not their mistakes, but their own altar, their own honest admission that there was something they did not know.
Then he describes God in words a Greek could follow. The God who made the world doesn't live in temples made by hands, and needs nothing from us, since he gives everyone life and breath.

teach.h: NOT FAR FROM ANY OF US.
teach.b: He made all nations from one, so that they would seek him, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from any of us.

teach.h: IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.
teach.b: Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Paul even quotes their own poets: we are also his offspring. Those words come from the Greek poet Aratus, and Paul uses them to build a bridge.
Only at the end does he speak of repentance, a day of judgment, and a man God raised from the dead.
At the word resurrection, some laugh.
Some say, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, including Dionysius, a member of the court, and a woman named Damaris.
The Catholic Church draws on this speech when it teaches that other religions often reflect a ray of the truth, and that God is near to every person who seeks.

how: Catholic teaching, especially the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, speaks with respect of what is true and holy in other religions, and Catholics remember Dionysius the Areopagite as a saint.

games.q: you're Paul on the Areopagus, before Athens's philosophers, in a city full of altars. how do you begin?
o: list what's wrong with their gods.
start with their own altar to an unknown God.
speak only from the Hebrew scriptures.
games.why: he praises how religious they are, points to their own altar, and quotes their own poets before he speaks of the resurrection.

practice: Think about the culture around you this week, a song stuck in your head, a show, a piece of art, a sports moment, and look for an altar in it, so to speak: some longing, some question, some reach toward something bigger that it never quite names.
Paul looked at a city full of statues and found a doorway; let one doorway in yours come to mind. If you pray, remember that in him we live, and move, and are, even here.

wordCard.voice: Areopagus. The hill in Athens where Paul was asked to explain his message, and where he began from an altar inscribed to an unknown god. Today's word.
